record.title: Google Home MCP exposes real device-state and control tools to AI clients in early access
record.summary: Google Home’s early-access MCP server connects compatible AI clients to real smart-home data and actions. Google’s developer documentation lists tools for discovering homes and devices, reading live state and history, and issuing device-control commands. It warns that an agent connected to a real home can control devices, describes rate limits and sensitive-action protections such as blocking door unlocking, and requires client permission before execution. Access requires a Premium Advanced subscription and approved project; automation creation was not yet supported on the page updated September 21. These are documented product capabilities and safeguards, not an independent test of enforcement or deployed use.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google documentation describes an early-access Home MCP server that lets compatible AI clients inspect home structures, device resources, live device states and historical events, and issue parameterized device-control actions.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Google documentation warns that connecting a real home allows an AI agent to control devices; it lists rate limits and protections including prohibiting sensitive actions such as unlocking doors, and says tool execution permission is granted through the client.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The inspected Google developer page labels Home MCP Early Access, says a Google Home Premium Advanced subscription and project approval are prerequisites, and records that automation creation was not yet supported as of its 2026-09-21 update.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent test confirms that the stated sensitive-action restrictions and user-consent controls are enforced across tools and client implementations.
The early-access documentation does not establish deployment scale, reliability or household-level effects.

brief.importance_rationale: If used as documented, the interface gives AI clients a direct path to inspect and actuate consumer home devices, changing the physical-action boundary for general-purpose agents. The consequence is meaningful for household safety and authorization design; the source is early-access product documentation and does not show adoption or tested safety performance.
limitations: This record covers documented product functionality, not measured agent capability or real-world deployment outcomes.
Google warns users that agents connected to real homes can behave unexpectedly; user review and revocation remain part of the documented model.

technical.claimed_result: Google documents an early-access service exposing home discovery, state/history queries and device actions through MCP-compatible clients.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public developer documentation specifies the available tool classes, prerequisites, warnings, execution-permission step and known limitations; the research desk did not connect to or test a home.
technical.mechanism: An MCP server proxies Google Home API resources and parameterized actions to a compatible AI client after OAuth configuration and user authorization.
technical.regime: Early-access Google Home MCP, requiring Google Home Premium Advanced, a Google Cloud project and approval; listed clients include Antigravity, Claude Cowork and OpenClaw.
technical.reproducibility: The developer guide is public. The service was not configured or tested; actual action enforcement and failure behavior remain unmeasured.
technical.strongest_baseline: Google’s documentation describes ordinary Home API access and the MCP proxy. No matched evaluation against direct API integrations or competing home-control agents was found.

brief.title: Google Home MCP exposes real device-state and control tools to AI clients in early access
brief.why_it_matters: This is a concrete path from general-purpose agents to physical device control in consumer environments. The practical boundary depends on the tool schema, authorization and server-side action restrictions, so the documented safeguards and their tested enforcement matter more than the MCP label alone.
